basis: New mission, no workbook source. Facts: 2016 DPP 'nuclear-free homeland' platform, written into the 2017 Electricity Act revision alongside the '20-30-50' 2025 generation-mix target; Maanshan Reactor 2 (Taiwan's last operating reactor) shut down 17 May 2025, ending nuclear power which had supplied ~4.2% of 2024 generation (288 TWh total, of which 42.4% gas / 39.3% coal / 11.6% renewables); 23 August 2025 referendum (Proposal No. 21) on restarting Maanshan: 74.2% yes among ~5.8M votes cast (~4.3M yes vs ~1.5M no) but failed procedurally because yes-votes fell short of the legal threshold of one quarter of registered voters (~5M of ~20M); Taiwan imports ~97% of its primary energy, with usable reserves estimated at about two weeks; Taipower accumulated losses of ~NT$418 billion, September 2025 rate rise ~3.12% (smaller than the 5-10% first proposed); 'energy trilemma' (security/equity/sustainability) framing per World Energy Council. Neutral on the nuclear debate throughout: trade-offs presented for all three options (restart, accelerate renewables, lean on gas), no side endorsed. Register per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. Authored by Claude directly (Gemini 3.1 Pro was unavailable for this mission's draft pass due to an API quota limit reached mid-session; content was hand-written to the same standard and iteratively verified against scripts/quality.py and scripts/grammar_range.py).

slides.1: On May 17, 2025, Taiwan turned off its last nuclear reactor. Just three months later, voters were asked to turn it back on completely. So what really changed?
slides.2: SDG 7 means safe, reliable, modern energy for everyone. Today we look at nuclear power through one simple idea. There are three goals, and they are hard to reach together.
slides.3: This story starts about ten years ago. In 2016, Taiwan chose a bold new plan. There would be no nuclear power after 2025. Today we look back at that long countdown.
slides.4: On May 17, 2025, Maanshan's last reactor shut down. This ended over 40 years of nuclear power here. Nuclear made only 4 percent of our power in 2024.
slides.5: Gas and coal made over 80 percent of our power in 2024. Nuclear then stopped. Gas and coal filled most of that gap, not renewable energy.
slides.6: People's views also moved. In August 2025, most voters who voted said yes to the plant. But not enough people voted, so the vote failed by law.
slides.7: What did Taiwan build instead? Over the past ten years, Taiwan added new gas terminals. It also built more wind turbines and solar panels.
slides.8: Nuclear and clean energy both release almost no carbon. Coal and gas release much more. So using more coal and gas raises Taiwan's total carbon output.
slides.9: Nuclear power runs all day and night, no matter the weather. Solar and wind power change with the sun and wind constantly. That makes the electric grid harder to balance.
slides.10: One option is to restart the reactor. This could cut carbon and cost fast, but it needs new safety inspections. Nobody agrees on how long that should take.
slides.11: A second option is building clean energy and storage faster. This choice is popular and very green. But it is already behind its own plan.
slides.12: A third option is using more imported gas as a bridge fuel. It is cleaner than coal. But Taiwan already imports almost all of its energy.
slides.13: Taiwan has only about two weeks of energy reserves. That means we cannot lose any power source easily. If one ship is delayed, that safety margin gets even smaller.
slides.14: Taipower has lost huge amounts of money for years. If prices stay too low, the company cannot pay for new power plants and storage.
slides.15: The carbon math still has to work. Even without enough new clean power, Taiwan must cut carbon fast. Otherwise gas and coal use will keep rising.
slides.16: So no single energy choice wins on all three goals. A safer choice can cost much more money. A cheaper choice can raise carbon. That is the real trilemma.
slides.17: To wrap up, Taiwan ended nuclear power right on time. Then voters almost changed that choice months later. The trilemma shows why neither choice was ever simple.
slides.18: This matters to you directly, right here in this room. Future engineers will design the reactors, grids and storage. Slogans will not do that work for us.
slides.19: Read the real numbers before you choose a side. Ask what problem each technology actually solves. Do not just pick a team to cheer for.
slides.20: The next vote, or the next reactor design, will eventually be decided by data or by loud slogans. Let's choose data instead. That choice is what should end this talk.
